title: Anchoring Bias — Why the First Number You Hear Controls Every Decision After It
title_variations: The First Number Wins: How Anchoring Hijacks Every Negotiation
Tversky, Kahneman, and the Price You Cannot Unhear
Why List Price, Sticker Price, and Salary Offers Are the Same Trap
description:
In 1974, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman demonstrated that a random number — spun on a wheel of fortune — could shift estimates of African nations in the United Nations by twenty percentage points. They called the pattern arbitrary coherence: the first number you encounter becomes a mental anchor, and every judgment afterward adjusts insufficiently away from it.

This documentary traces anchoring through three transactions you will face repeatedly — a car dealership negotiation, a salary offer, and a real estate listing — to show that the same psychological mechanism operates at every price point. Dan Ariely's later experiments confirm what negotiators already exploit: whoever sets the anchor first controls the range of what feels reasonable.

Subscribe to Wired Broke for weekly behavioral finance documentaries on the biases your brain hides from you.
story_spine: The first number in any transaction — sticker price, list price, opening salary — silently sets the range of what feels fair; Tversky and Kahneman proved the mechanism is automatic, and Ariely showed professionals fall for it too.
stakes: Whoever speaks first in a negotiation does not just state a price — they install the coordinates your brain will use for every counteroffer that follows.
midpoint_reversal: The anchor does not need to be relevant or honest — Kahneman's wheel of fortune was random, yet it still bent expert estimates; your car dealer's sticker works the same way.
open_loops: Why does a spinning wheel change how many countries you think are in the United Nations?
What do a thirty-two-thousand-dollar sedan and a four-hundred-thousand-dollar house have in common psychologically?
Can you negotiate rationally after the first number is already in your head?

hook.text: Saturday morning. A car lot in Phoenix. The salesman quotes thirty-four thousand nine hundred dollars — MSRP on the window sticker you have been staring at since you pulled in. You counter at thirty-one. You feel clever. You have no idea the sticker was the entire game. Tuesday afternoon. A hiring manager slides an offer across a table: eighty-two thousand dollars base salary. You ask for ninety. You feel bold. The eighty-two thousand was never a forecast of your worth. It was a coordinate. Thursday evening. A couple walks through a colonial listed at four hundred twenty-five thousand. They offer four hundred. They feel disciplined. The listing agent knew the anchor would pull every bid upward from a number chosen to frame the room. Three transactions. Three price points. One mechanism. The first number you hear does not inform your decision. It controls it.

scenes.narration: Nineteen seventy-four. Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman run an experiment that should not work — and does every time. Subjects arrive at a classroom. They spin a wheel of fortune rigged to stop only on ten or sixty-five. Then they answer two questions: is the percentage of African nations in the United Nations higher or lower than that number? And what is your best estimate? The wheel is irrelevant. Everyone knows it. Yet subjects who spin sixty-five produce median estimates around forty-five percent. Subjects who spin ten produce estimates around twenty-five percent. A difference of twenty percentage points from a random number. Tversky and Kahneman call it anchoring and adjustment: you start from the anchor, then adjust — but you stop adjusting too soon. The first number creates coherence where none existed.

scenes.narration: They label the phenomenon arbitrary coherence. Arbitrary because the anchor can be random, irrelevant, or absurd. Coherence because once it lands, your mind builds a plausible story around it. You do not experience yourself as copying a wheel. You experience yourself as reasoning. That gap — between feeling rational and behaving anchored — is the entire behavioral finance revolution in one experiment. Kahneman would spend decades showing that experts anchor too. Judges anchor on sentences suggested by prosecutors. Real estate agents anchor on list prices. Accountants anchor on prior-year figures. The bias is not a retail investor problem. It is a human cognition problem.

scenes.narration: Dan Ariely extends the work in the two thousands with experiments that feel uncomfortably personal. MIT students bid on items — wine, chocolate, books — but first write the last two digits of their Social Security numbers. High digits produce higher bids. Low digits produce lower bids. The anchor is not even a price. It is noise dressed as a number. Ariely publishes the results in Predictably Irrational and argues markets are less rational than economics textbooks assume because anchors live inside every catalog page, every suggested tip on a payment screen, every was price beside a sale tag. The first number does not have to be true. It only has to be first.

scenes.narration: Here is the mechanism in plain language. Stage one: an anchor arrives — sticker, list price, opening offer, suggested donation. Stage two: your brain treats it as a starting point, not a fact. Stage three: you adjust toward what you believe is correct — but adjustment is lazy, incomplete, and confident. You walk away feeling you thought independently. In reality you moved from their number, not from zero. Car dealers know this. Recruiters know this. Listing agents know this. The science names what negotiators have practiced for centuries: whoever sets the anchor first owns the frame.

scenes.narration: The car dealership. A buyer named Marcus spends two weeks researching a midsize SUV — safety ratings, fuel economy, resale value. He arrives prepared. The window sticker reads thirty-four thousand nine hundred. Marcus has a target: thirty thousand flat. The salesman opens at sticker, then drops to thirty-three five — a concession that feels like a gift. Marcus counters thirty-one. They settle at thirty-two two. Marcus drives home believing he beat the dealer by twenty-seven hundred dollars. But the negotiation never started at zero. It started at thirty-four nine. Every counteroffer orbited the sticker. Industry data shows buyers who see a high MSRP anchor negotiate in a narrower band above true invoice cost. Marcus did not buy a car. He adjusted from a number the manufacturer printed to create exactly this feeling of victory.

scenes.narration: The salary offer. Priya interviews for a senior product role at a tech company. Twelve years of experience. Market research in her notebook suggests a fair range between ninety-five and one hundred ten thousand for her city and level. The hiring manager opens at eighty-two thousand plus a ten percent bonus target. Priya feels a flash of insult — then relief when they move to eighty-eight. She counters at ninety-four. They close at ninety-one. Priya accepts, grateful for the climb. But the anchor was eighty-two, not her research. Studies on salary negotiation show first offers predict final outcomes more strongly than candidate qualifications. The company saved nineteen thousand dollars against her ceiling while Priya felt she won. The number on the table was never an estimate of value. It was a floor disguised as an offer.

scenes.narration: The real estate listing. David and Elena tour a suburban colonial. Comparable sales in the neighborhood — the comps agents are supposed to use — cluster around three hundred eighty to four hundred thousand. The listing price is four hundred twenty-five. The agent says the sellers are motivated but priced for the market. David and Elena offer four hundred, five percent below ask. The sellers counter at four eighteen. They settle at four oh eight. They feel they stole the house. Ariely and other researchers find that even professional agents appraise homes closer to arbitrary list prices than to objective comp data when anchors are manipulated in experiments. The four twenty-five listing was not prophecy. It was a lighthouse placed above the reef — every ship adjusts course toward the light.

scenes.narration: Place the three stories side by side. Marcus saved twenty-seven hundred from a sticker. Priya gained nine thousand from an opening offer. David and Elena saved seventeen thousand from a list price. Different scales — thirty-two thousand, ninety-one thousand, four hundred eight thousand — identical psychology. In each case the buyer believed they negotiated hard. In each case the seller chose the first number. Tversky and Kahneman showed the anchor can be random. The car lot, the HR department, and the listing agent show it can be strategic. Arbitrary coherence becomes engineered coherence. And your confidence after the deal is part of the trap — the feeling of victory prevents you from asking what you would have paid if you had never heard their number first.

scenes.narration: Kahneman's research suggests defense is harder than awareness. Once an anchor is in memory, suppressing it takes cognitive effort most negotiations do not allow. But three practices measurably help. First, generate your anchor before you hear theirs — write your number on paper before the salesman speaks, before the offer letter arrives, before the open house. Second, reject the frame explicitly. Ariely recommends asking whether the opening figure is based on comps, invoice, or budget — forcing the other side to justify breaks the spell of arbitrary coherence. Third, use bracketing with independent data: invoice cost from a third-party site, salary bands from verified surveys, sold-home comps from county records. You are not trying to forget their number. You are building a second number that competes for authority.

scenes.narration: Watch for the concessions trap — the second anchor. The dealer drops from thirty-four nine to thirty-three five. HR moves from eighty-two to eighty-eight. The seller counters from four twenty-five to four eighteen. Each concession feels like progress. Behavioral economists call this the contrast effect stacking onto anchoring: a bad deal beside a worse deal looks generous. Marcus, Priya, and David and Elena all received concessions. None received independent pricing. The dealer's second number is still an anchor. The revised offer is still a frame. The counteroffer is designed to make you stop adjusting exactly where they want.

scenes.narration: The deeper lesson from Tversky and Kahneman is not that you are gullible. It is that adjustment is insufficient by design. The mind treats anchoring as a shortcut — a way to estimate under uncertainty. That shortcut was useful on savannas where guessing fast mattered more than guessing precisely. In modern markets, the shortcut is harvested. Every suggested tip percentage, every was price, every premium tier on a pricing page is an anchor tested for conversion. Dan Ariely's auction experiments and Kahneman's wheel of fortune differ in setting but not in structure: a number arrives, your brain complies, your confidence follows. The first number is never neutral. It is always a claim on your judgment.

scenes.narration: Marcus still loves his SUV. Priya still enjoys the job. David and Elena still raise their kids in the colonial. Anchoring does not mean every deal is a loss. It means the outcome was shaped by a number you did not choose. Thirty-four nine hundred. Eighty-two thousand. Four twenty-five. Three anchors, three lives, one mechanism operating at every price point in every transaction you will ever have. Tversky and Kahneman named it in nineteen seventy-four. Ariely proved you cannot willpower your way past it. The defense is procedural: decide your number first, bring independent comps, and recognize that the opening figure is not information — it is strategy. Whoever speaks first does not just open the negotiation. They anchor your mind.

outro.text: Your brain does not begin at zero. It begins at the first number someone else puts in the room. Tversky and Kahneman proved it with a wheel of fortune.
